lesson.menu_desc: Concerns and limits: "I'd rather you + past form", and a soft start, a clear middle and a way forward -- 27 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 27 — Navigating Difficult Conversations
lesson.title_tag: Professor View — Vanessa Giuriati | Lesson 27 — Navigating Difficult Conversations
lesson.grammar_point: I'd rather you / I'd prefer it if + past form (asking someone else to change)

listenings.text: For years I avoided difficult conversations, and I paid for it. I would let small things slide until they became big things, and then I would explode at the worst possible moment. What finally helped me was a simple structure that a colleague called the sandwich. First, a soft opening, so the other person does not feel attacked. There is something I wanted to bring up. Do you have a minute? Then the honest part, in one or two sentences, without apologizing for it. The report was late three times this month, and it affects my team. And finally, a way forward. I would rather we agreed on a new deadline than kept pretending. The trick is the middle. Most people make the opening and the close so long that the real message disappears. Keep the bread thin. The filling is the point.

I am the kind of person who says yes to everything, so learning to set boundaries took me a long time. The first one was small. I told my manager I would not answer messages after eight in the evening, unless it was an emergency. I was terrified. I expected a long discussion. Instead, she said, fine, thanks for telling me. That was it. What I learned is that most people are not against your boundaries. They simply do not know where they are until you speak up. The hard part is not the conversation. It is the six weeks you spend avoiding it. Now, when something bothers me, I give myself forty-eight hours. If I still care after two days, I address it. If I do not, I let it go, and I really let it go.

extra_audio.text: First, I ask for a minute and say there is something I wanted to bring up. Then I name my concern in one or two clear sentences. After that, I say what I would rather happen: I'd rather you told me earlier. Next, I listen to the other person, and we work through the problem together. In the end, we agree on one clear next step, so nobody lets it slide again.
